newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- JAN 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- JAN 8.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--The US and Western European governments have expressed their displeasure at Cyprus's decision to buy Russian S-300 missiles, citing the danger of a military clash on the island-republic. Nicosia, however, has responded with calm and decisiveness, stressing its right to self-defence, while Athens made clear yesterday that it supported the Cypriot government's decision and calling on those protesting to direct their opposition to the Turkish side to accept Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides's proposal for the full demilitarisation of the island.

--A new cycle of strike action will begin within the month. Prime Minister Costas Simitis's hard line on the recent farmers' blockade appears to have had little effect on other social groups, while farmers will decide on a return to the frontlines after the Council of Agricultural Policy convenes on Friday.

--An initial agreement thrashed out yesterday between conservative opposition New Democracy leader Miltiades Evert, challenger George Souflias and ND deputy leader Ioannis Varvitsiotis to hold the party's congress in late March is expected to be approved by the Executive Council today.
--Greeks' love affair with automobiles continues, undeterred by economic hardship. New car sales reached 140,000 in 1996, up 12 percent from 1995 figures.

--The government and all political parties were categorical yesterday in their rejection of protests over Cyprus's missiles purchase. Athens and Nicosia rejected the US demarche while Clinton's special emissary Kerry Cavanaugh is on his way to Athens, Ankara and Nicosia.
--The Greek police say they would have caught the burglary gang terrorising northeastern Attica if it were not for the avalanche of publicity in recent days.
--Final changes to the civil servants uniform pay scale were revealed to the public by Deputy Finance Minister Nikos Christodoulakis yesterday to a lukewarm response from the union, ADEDY.

--The new pay scale means increases of 6-10 percent for all civil servants. Another 22 bonuses will be maintained, while teachers and workers at state hospitals will receive other benefits. Overtime, however, will be cut back drastically.

--Turkey is planning on striking north of the island of Samos at one of the islands of the central and northern Aegean, in accordance with a 1995 plan. Turkey yesterday began exercises in the central Aegean in the region between the islands of Skyros and Hios.

--Light at the end of the tunnel for New Democracy as Souflias takes a more conciliatory line. Deputies and party officials said they were happy with the outcome of yesterday's meeting. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
